anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and indexing choices are mis-aligned with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient data access regardless of statistics freshness.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are adequate, often due to cost-model or plan-cache issues.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or replay log records as fast as the primary generates them.

When all three root causes are present, the system suffers a compound performance and availability degradation. Queries on the primary exhibit excessive full scans, non-covering index lookups, or poorly chosen join methods, inflating CPU and I/O. These bloated executions enlarge transaction logs and generate more redo, while inefficient plans may also hold locks longer and bundle more row changes per statement. The oversized and plan-inflated redo stream then overwhelms replicas whose apply threads are already struggling, causing rapidly widening replication lag, persistent replica read staleness, and a rising backlog of retained log segments on the primary. Meanwhile, sporadic plan flips further vary redo volume and execution latency, making lag patterns erratic and troubleshooting harder.

Causally, poor schema/index design creates wide scans and row fetch amplification. The optimizer, already faced with ill-suited structures, may still pick sub-optimal plans, multiplying the work per transaction. This extra work translates directly into larger and burstier redo generation. Replication pipelines must ship and apply every changed row; therefore, the inflated and uneven log traffic stresses network, disk, and apply CPU on replicas, triggering or worsening synchronization slowdowns. As replicas lag, they retain older log segments, preventing log recycling on the primary and increasing primary storage pressure, which in turn can slow production queries even more. The intertwined feedback loop—inefficient data access, bad plan choices, and stalled replication—magnifies latency, resource consumption, and risk of failover gaps beyond what any single anomaly would cause alone.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
